segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They saw that some of his disciples were eating their bread with defiled hands, that is, unwashed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Pharisees, and indeed all the Jews, do not eat unless they wash their hands with the fist, holding to the tradition of the elders;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when they come from the marketplace they do not eat unless they immerse themselves. And there are many other things that they have received to hold to: the immersing of cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and dining couches.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Pharisees and the scribes asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat their bread with defiled hands?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: in vain do they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You let go of the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How well you set aside the commandment of God in order to keep your tradition!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must be put to death.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you say that if someone tells his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban,’ that is, a gift,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: then you no longer let him do anything for his father or mother,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: nullifying the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And you do many things like this.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he called the crowd to him again and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Listen to me, all of you, and understand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: There is nothing outside a person that by going in can defile that person; rather, the things that come out of a person are what defile the person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had left the crowd and gone into a house, his disciples asked him about the parable.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are you too so lacking in understanding? Do you not see that nothing that goes into a person from outside can defile that person,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: because it goes not into the heart but into the stomach, and then out into the latrine?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Thus he declared all foods clean.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What comes out of a person, that is what defiles the person.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For from within, out of people’s hearts, come evil designs: acts of sexual immorality, thefts, murders,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: adulteries, acts of greed, wicked deeds, deceit, debauchery, a grudging eye, slander, arrogance, folly.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: All these wicked things come from within and defile the person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From there he set out and went away to the region of Tyre. He went into a house and did not want anyone to know it, yet he could not escape notice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him at once, and she came and fell down at his feet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the woman was a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth, and she kept asking him to drive the demon out of her daughter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let the children eat their fill first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Because of that answer, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went away to her home and found the child lying on the bed and the demon gone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Leaving the region of Tyre again, he went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the middle of the region of the Decapolis.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought him a man who was deaf and could hardly speak, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking him aside, away from the crowd, he put his fingers into the man’s ears, and after spitting he touched the man’s tongue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Ephphatha,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which means, “Be opened.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And his ears were opened, the bond on his tongue was loosed, and he began to speak plainly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He ordered them to tell no one; but the more he ordered them, all the more they proclaimed it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were astounded beyond all measure, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has done everything well; he makes both the deaf hear and the speechless speak.”

notes.note: The Greek word ordinarily means “common” or “shared.” In Jewish Greek it had come to mean ritually impure, the opposite of holy, and Mark explains it for readers unfamiliar with that usage. The issue is ritual purity, not hygiene; the related verb is rendered “defile” from verse 15 onward.

The Greek says literally “with the fist,” and what that meant is uncertain. Suggestions include washing with a cupped hand, with a fistful of water, up to the wrist, or by rubbing a fist in the other palm; many versions paraphrase as “thoroughly” or “ceremonially.” Some manuscripts replace the word with one meaning “often,” which suggests that early copyists were also puzzled.

The verb is the one elsewhere rendered “baptize”; its ordinary sense is to dip or immerse, and it is a different word from the one for washing hands in verse 3. Most versions say “wash,” and the standard lexicons allow that sense for ritual purification; the related noun is rendered “immersing” later in the verse. Some early manuscripts read “sprinkle” instead. The clause could also mean that they immerse what they bring from the marketplace, though that is the less common view.

notes.traditional: tables (KJV); dining couches; omitted in many modern versions
notes.note: The words “and dining couches” are absent from several important early manuscripts, and many modern versions omit them or move them to a footnote. The SBLGNT includes them. The word can mean a bed or the couch on which diners reclined.

Corban is a Hebrew word for an offering dedicated to God, which Mark translates for his readers as “gift.” Declaring property Corban placed it under a vow, so that the person named—here a parent—could no longer benefit from it. Exactly how such vows worked in practice in this period is debated.

Verse 16 (“If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear”) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not in the SBLGNT text, so the numbering passes from 15 to 17. It was probably added by copyists from similar sayings elsewhere in Mark.

notes.phrase: Thus he declared all foods clean.
notes.traditional: purging all meats (KJV); Thus he declared all foods clean (most modern versions)
notes.note: The Greek is a brief participial phrase, literally “cleansing all foods.” In the earliest manuscripts the participle is masculine, and most scholars connect it with “he said” in verse 18, as Mark’s own comment on what Jesus’s teaching implied. Later manuscripts have a neuter form, which makes the phrase part of Jesus’s words about digestion purging food; the King James Version follows that reading.

Literally “an evil eye,” a Semitic idiom for a stingy or envious disposition (compare Deuteronomy 15:9 and Matthew 20:15). The literal phrase now suggests a curse cast by a look, which is not the point here. Many modern versions simply say “envy.”

“Greek” here marks the woman as a Gentile of Greek language and culture, not as someone from Greece. “Syrophoenician” identifies her as a native of the Phoenician coast, which belonged to the Roman province of Syria.

The Greek word is a diminutive, and some take it to mean small house dogs or puppies, softening the saying. Diminutives in the Greek of this period had often lost their force, and Mark uses several in this passage, so many scholars doubt that any softening is intended. In the image, “the children” are Israel and the dogs are Gentiles.

The Greek word was the ordinary respectful address to a man, like “sir,” and also the word for “Lord.” From a Gentile stranger the everyday sense is the natural one, though many versions print “Lord” and Mark’s readers may well have heard more in it. In the text followed here, this is the only place in Mark where Jesus is addressed with this word.

Sidon lies north of Tyre, while the Sea of Galilee and the Decapolis lie to the southeast, so the route described is a wide loop through largely Gentile territory. The Decapolis (“Ten Cities”) was a group of Hellenistic cities, most of them east of the Jordan.

notes.traditional: had an impediment in his speech
notes.note: This rare word occurs only here in the New Testament and once in the Greek version of Isaiah (35:6), in a passage promising that the ears of the deaf will be opened and the tongue of the speechless will sing. Mark’s choice of the word, together with the crowd’s acclamation in verse 37, probably points to that prophecy.

candidates.reason: The κοινός/κοινόω word group for ritual impurity recurs in Matthew, Acts, Romans, Hebrews, and Revelation, and versions vary between “defile,” “make unclean,” “common,” and “profane.”
Recurs across the Gospels, Acts, Paul, and Revelation, with versions split between “fornication,” “sexual immorality,” and “unchastity,” and its scope is debated.
The word covers both abusive speech against people and blasphemy against God, and readers need a consistent policy on when each English word is used.
The vocative addressed to Jesus by strangers can be “Sir” or “Lord,” and the choice needs to be made consistently across the Gospels and their parallels.
“Scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers, whereas the word names recognized experts in the Law; alternatives such as “legal experts” or “teachers of the law” are in use.
